bibl.title: Changes in human brain dynamics during behavioral priming and repetition suppression

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The latter results indicate that repetition suppression and behavioral priming are associated with strengthening of top-down network influences on perceptual processing, consistent with predictive coding models of repetition suppression, and they support a central role for changes in large-scale cortical dynamics in achieving more efficient and rapid behavioral responses.

span.label: behavioural priming and repetition suppression
span.quote: Behavioral responses to a perceptual stimulus are typically faster with repeated exposure to the stimulus (behavioral priming).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Here, we used the unparalleled precision of electrocorticography (ECoG) to analyze the timing and magnitude of task-related changes in neural activation and propagation while patients named novel vs repeated visual objects.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: With repetition the cortex's generative model predicts the stimulus better, so top-down predictive input grows stronger and the prediction-error cells it suppresses fire less, which is what is measured as repetition suppression
span.quote: As the model improves its predictions with stimulus repetition and experience, the top-down input grows stronger and activity in cells that encode prediction error decreases, yielding repetition suppression.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Strengthened top-down propagation from left prefrontal cortex drives down activation in ventral occipito-temporal cortex and elsewhere, producing repetition suppression
span.quote: These findings are suggestive of a role for repetition-related top-down propagation from LPFC in driving effects on repetition suppression that are observed in VOTC and elsewhere.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: At sensorimotor and superior-temporal sites the apparent temporal shift is not a change in perception but a consequence of the shorter speaking latency: the activity is locked to the response, so aligning to response onset abolishes the shift
span.quote: This shift, however, was no longer apparent when cortical signals were aligned to response onset, suggesting that activation at these sites was linked to response processing and that the temporal shift was due to shorter latencies to respond to repeated stimuli.

span.label: Repetition enhancement was significant only at individual sites; group analyses failed to reach significance in any region of interest, possibly through timing variability and uneven sampling.
span.quote: Although we observed statistically significant RE at 30 recording sites across 10 patients, our group analyses did not reach statistical significance for any of the regions of interest, potentially due to variations in the timing and magnitude of RE across patients, as well as inter-individual variations in spatial sampling of our regions of interest.

span.label: Only very short (few-second) repetition delays were examined, while the models at stake concern much longer delays.
span.quote: It will be important to examine repetition effects on neural dynamics over much longer repetition delays than examined here (a few seconds), as both behavioral priming and repetition suppression have been observed over delays of hours and days, and these longer delays are of paramount importance to models positing long-lasting changes to cortical representations (e.g. perceptual sharpening and predictive coding models).

span.label: High gamma responses cannot adjudicate models that posit changes in single-neuron tuning, such as the sharpening model.
span.quote: Although these responses cannot be used to test models that posit changes in the tuning preferences of individual neurons (e.g. sharpening), they can be used to measure neural dynamics at time scales relevant to the evaluation of other models.

span.label: Electrode placement was clinically, not experimentally, determined, constraining which sites could show each repetition effect.
span.quote: It is important to note that implantation of electrodes was performed solely according to clinical needs.

span.label: Electrode placement was clinically determined, so the sites at which each repetition effect could be detected were constrained by each patient's coverage.
span.quote: Therefore, the numbers of sites revealing repetition suppression, repetition enhancement, or temporal shift were limited by the electrode locations unique to each patient.

span.label: Repetition enhancement was significant at individual sites but failed to reach significance in any region-of-interest group analysis.
span.quote: Although we observed statistically significant RE at 30 recording sites across 10 patients, our group analyses did not reach statistical significance for any of the regions of interest, potentially due to variations in the timing and magnitude of RE across patients, as well as inter-individual variations in spatial sampling of our regions of interest.

span.label: Only short (few-second) repetition delays were tested, whereas the models at issue concern long-lasting representational change.
span.quote: It will be important to examine repetition effects on neural dynamics over much longer repetition delays than examined here (a few seconds), as both behavioral priming and repetition suppression have been observed over delays of hours and days, and these longer delays are of paramount importance to models positing long-lasting changes to cortical representations (e.g. perceptual sharpening and predictive coding models).

span.label: The design and analyses cannot adjudicate the sharpening or synchrony models.
span.quote: Appropriate tests of both the sharpening and the synchrony model will require further studies with somewhat different methods ( Gotts et al. , 2015 ).

span.label: The Granger-causality framework for time series is taken over, as event related causality built on multivariate autoregressive models, to estimate the direction and timing of neural propagation between cortical recording sites.
span.quote: we evaluated changes in the propagation of high gamma activity using a recently developed technique – event related causality (ERC), based on the concept of Granger causality, to measure the timing, magnitude and directionality of task-related changes in neural propagation across cortical networks activated during visual object naming

span.label: The predictive coding account the paper adopts treats the cortex itself as a hierarchical generative Bayesian statistical model, with top-down predictions and bottom-up prediction error.
span.quote: In this model, the cortex is considered a form of hierarchical generative Bayesian statistical model.

span.label: object names matched for word frequency, and the lists of repeated versus novel objects counterbalanced across patients
span.note: eliminates: that a difference between novel and repeated objects is a difference in word frequency, or a property of which particular objects happened to land in which list
span.quote: Object names were matched for word frequency, and lists of repeated versus non-repeated (novel) objects were counterbalanced across patients.

span.label: behavioral priming
span.quote: Many studies of the neural bases for behavioral priming have encountered an interesting paradox: in spite of faster behavioral responses, repeated stimuli usually elicit weaker neural responses (repetition suppression)

span.label: repetition suppression
span.quote: Stimulus repetition was associated with faster verbal responses and decreased neural activation (repetition suppression) in ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) and left prefrontal cortex (LPFC)

span.label: repetition enhancement
span.quote: Interestingly, we also observed increased neural activation (repetition enhancement) in LPFC and other recording sites

span.label: electrocorticography
span.quote: Several neurophysiological models have been proposed to resolve this paradox, but noninvasive techniques for human studies have had insufficient spatial-temporal precision for testing their predictions. Here, we used the unparalleled precision of electrocorticography

span.label: predictive coding
span.quote: Repetition suppression occurred in ventral temporal and left prefrontal cortex Early top-down neural propagation preceded repetition suppression These results provide support for predictive coding in behavioral priming

span.label: THE SAME PARADOX Gotts2012 REVIEWS, AND THIS IS THE EXPERIMENT IT ASKED FOR. Gotts said the four candidate models were `in need of testing`; this paper says why they had not been tested - `noninvasive techniques for human studies have had INSUFFICIENT SPATIAL-TEMPORAL PRECISION for testing their predictions` - and then supplies the precision with electrocorticography. A review naming a gap and a study filling it, two records in one corpus
span.quote: Several neurophysiological models have been proposed to resolve this paradox, but noninvasive techniques for human studies have had insufficient spatial-temporal precision for testing their predictions. Here, we used the unparalleled precision of electrocorticography

span.label: THREE EFFECTS, NOT TWO. Beside suppression the study finds repetition ENHANCEMENT at some sites and a TEMPORAL SHIFT to earlier responses at others - `repetition suppression (RS) at some sites, and repetition enhancement (RE) in others, the latter often followed by repetition suppression (~600 ms)`. The paradox as usually stated has two terms; measured at this resolution the cortex does three different things, sometimes in sequence at one site
span.quote: we observed a more complex pattern of changes, reflecting repetition suppression (RS) at some sites, and repetition enhancement (RE) in others, the latter often followed by repetition suppression

span.label: AND THE NOVEL EFFECT DOES NOT SURVIVE THE GROUP ANALYSIS, IN THE PAPER'S OWN WORDS: `Group analyses aggregating recording sites with statistically significant repetition enhancement (RE) DID NOT REACH STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE for VOTC, LPFC, or OAS.` So RE is a per-site observation, reported honestly as one, with the closing verdict that further investigation `is warranted` rather than that the effect is established. The result the abstract calls `interesting` is the one the results section declines to claim at group level
span.quote: Group analyses aggregating recording sites with statistically significant repetition enhancement (RE) did not reach statistical significance for VOTC, LPFC, or OAS

span.label: WHAT THE ELECTRODES COULD SEE IS A LIMIT ON WHAT WAS FOUND, and the paper says so: `the numbers of sites revealing repetition suppression, repetition enhancement, or temporal shift were LIMITED BY THE ELECTRODE LOCATIONS UNIQUE TO EACH PATIENT`. Coverage is clinical, not experimental - electrodes go where the epilepsy surgery needs them - so absence of an effect at a site is not evidence of its absence in that region. A sampling constraint that no amount of statistics repairs
span.quote: Therefore, the numbers of sites revealing repetition suppression, repetition enhancement, or temporal shift were limited by the electrode locations unique to each patient

span.label: builds-on → Ghuman et al. (2008) MEG study of LPFC-temporal phase locking during priming
span.quote: Our finding of early increased top-down propagation with repetition complements a previous study by Ghuman et al. (2008) using MEG, which reported enhanced phase-locking between LPFC and temporal cortex in low-beta frequencies (12–14 Hz) for repeated objects during object identification, beginning ~200 ms after stimulus onset.

span.label: contradicts → the “facilitation” model of repetition suppression (James et al., 2000; Henson, 2003)
span.quote: Importantly, we did not observe a consistent temporal shift in the temporal envelope of VOTC activation to earlier latencies, as predicted by the “facilitation” model.

span.label: extends → Ghuman et al. (2008) MEG study of top-down phase locking in priming
span.quote: Our finding of early increased top-down propagation with repetition complements a previous study by Ghuman et al. (2008) using MEG, which reported enhanced phase-locking between LPFC and temporal cortex in low-beta frequencies (12–14 Hz) for repeated objects during object identification, beginning ~200 ms after stimulus onset.

span.label: contradicts → the "facilitation" model of repetition suppression (James et al., 2000; Henson, 2003)
span.quote: Importantly, we did not observe a consistent temporal shift in the temporal envelope of VOTC activation to earlier latencies, as predicted by the “facilitation” model.

span.label: builds-on → the "predictive coding" model of repetition suppression and priming (Henson, 2003; Friston, 2005)
span.quote: The entire pattern of results is perhaps in best accordance with the “predictive coding” model of repetition suppression and priming ( Henson, 2003 ; Friston, 2005 ).

span.label: replicates → Marinkovic et al. (2003) MEG finding of a shift from repetition enhancement to repetition suppression
span.quote: This diversity occurred early, and sustained suppression followed, consistent with previous findings with MEG that repetition effects can shift from initial RE to RS ( Marinkovic et al. , 2003 ).

span.label: behavioral priming —contrasted-with→ repetition suppression
span.note: differs in: THE DIRECTION EACH MOVES ON THE SAME REPETITION - responses get FASTER while neural activity gets WEAKER. The paper calls it a paradox in the sentence that states it, and the whole study exists to resolve it · strength of the relation: 0.95 — The same contrast tagged on Gotts2012 forty minutes earlier, from a review; here it is from the experiment that tests it. Two records, one paradox, and the corpus can now hold the review's inventory beside the measurement.
span.quote: Many studies of the neural bases for behavioral priming have encountered an interesting paradox: in spite of faster behavioral responses, repeated stimuli usually elicit weaker neural responses (repetition suppression)

span.label: predictive coding —causes→ repetition suppression
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE EVIDENCE IS A TIMING CLAIM: the top-down propagation PRECEDED the suppression, which is what makes it a candidate cause rather than a correlate. Weighted 0.85 - `provide support for` is the paper's own strength, and precedence is necessary but not sufficient for the model.
span.quote: Repetition suppression occurred in ventral temporal and left prefrontal cortex Early top-down neural propagation preceded repetition suppression These results provide support for predictive coding in behavioral priming

span.label: repetition enhancement —distinct-from→ repetition suppression
span.note: differs in: THE SIGN OF THE NEURAL CHANGE AT A SITE - enhancement is more activity with repetition, suppression is less, and the two occur at different electrodes in the same patients, sometimes in sequence at one site with enhancement followed by suppression around 600 ms · strength of the relation: 0.8 — Weight 0.8 and NOT higher, because of the group analysis: RE `did not reach statistical significance for VOTC, LPFC, or OAS`. The distinction is real at individual sites and unestablished at group level, and the sense row carries that. Recording this at 0.95 would assert what the results section declines to claim.
span.quote: we observed a more complex pattern of changes, reflecting repetition suppression (RS) at some sites, and repetition enhancement (RE) in others, the latter often followed by repetition suppression

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: Behavioral priming effects were highly significant in a group analysis of all patients (paired t -test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons: t(9) = 6.015, p < 0.001, with each patient showing a numerical decrease in response time (RT) for repeated relative to novel trials (mean = 153 ms, and median = 128 ms).

span.label: sign test
span.quote: For each ECoG recording site in each patient, event-related changes in high gamma power relative to the pre-stimulus baseline were statistically tested separately for novel and repeated trials using a nonparametric sign test at every post-stimulus time point.

span.label: false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons
span.term: false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: Pooled variance over trials with novel or repeated stimuli, for each patient, was used for further two-sided paired t -tests ( p < 0.05, FDR corrected for multiple comparisons at every time point), for all patients combined.

span.label: one-tailed t-test
span.quote: Specifically, we tested for increases in responses to repeated stimuli as compared to novel stimuli, using a one-sided t-test with FDR correction.

span.label: multivariate autoregressive model order selection by Akaike Information Criterion
span.term: multivariate autoregressive model order selection by Akaike Information Criterion
span.quote: The model order p was determined using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: A 95% joint confidence interval was constructed for the difference between the estimates of connectivity during trials and the baseline estimate of connectivity.

span.label: multitaper spectral estimation
span.quote: Spectral power was extracted from ECoG signals, band-pass filtered in the 16–200 Hz range, in 128 ms long sliding windows with a 16 ms overlap, using a multi-taper algorithm from the Chronux toolbox

span.label: penalized spline regression
span.quote: ERC values were then obtained using statistical testing (penalized thin-plate spline) ( Ruppert et al. , 2003 ) to compare the estimates of connectivity during post-stimulus intervals to baseline connectivity estimates.

span.label: standard deviation and median absolute deviation
span.term: standard deviation and median absolute deviation
span.quote: Mean response times and their standard deviations, as well as median response times and median absolute deviations (MAD) for each patient for successful novel and repeated trials are shown in Table 2

span.label: Behavioral priming was accompanied by suppressed high gamma activity in ventral occipito-temporal cortex, left prefrontal cortex and other activated sites, plus a shift of activity to earlier time points in sensorimotor regions that mediate speaking.
span.quote: In the current study, we have shown that behavioral priming following short-term repetitions in humans is accompanied by suppression of neural activity in VOTC, LPFC, and other activated sites, as well as temporal shifts of activity to earlier time points in sensorimotor regions mediating verbal responses.

span.label: Repetition also increased activation at 30 sites in lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex, but never in ventral occipito-temporal cortex, so repetition enhancement and suppression occupy different territory.
span.quote: Repetition enhancement (RE) was observed in 30 sites located in lateral frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, but not in VOTC.

span.label: Repeated stimuli produced a statistically significant increase in high gamma propagation from left prefrontal cortex into ventral occipito-temporal cortex beginning about 100 ms after stimulus onset.
span.quote: This analysis revealed a statistically significant ( p < 0.05, FDR-corrected to q <.05) increase in propagation from LPFC to VOTC for repeated stimuli relative to novel stimuli, which started around 100 ms after stimulus onset

span.label: The repetition-related rise in top-down propagation became significant before repetition suppression appeared in VOTC, putting the top-down change first in the causal order.
span.quote: Note that the repetition-related increase in top-down propagation from LPFC to VOTC became significant numerically earlier than repetition suppression in VOTC did.

span.label: Within individual patients the dominant direction of flow reversed with repetition: novel stimuli drove propagation bottom-up from VOTC to LPFC, whereas repeated stimuli drove it top-down from LPFC to VOTC.
span.quote: In ERC analyses within individual patients we observed that for trials with novel stimuli, the most prominent neural propagation (ERC flow) was from VOTC to LPFC, with far less propagation in the opposite direction.

span.label: The facilitation model's central prediction failed in ventral occipito-temporal cortex: repeated trials showed no consistent shift of the activation envelope to earlier latencies, only a reduced peak and an earlier return to baseline.
span.quote: Importantly, we did not observe a consistent temporal shift in the temporal envelope of VOTC activation to earlier latencies, as predicted by the “facilitation” model.

span.label: Repetition suppression emerged in ventral occipito-temporal cortex at about 140 ms but only reached significance in left prefrontal cortex at about 280 ms.
span.quote: Interestingly, in group analyses of repetition suppression (RS), it became statistically significant in LPFC later (~ 280 ms, Fig. 3 center) than in VOTC (~ 140 ms, Fig. 3 left), with a slight time-shift in the peak activation in LPFC to earlier time points in the repeat condition

span.label: Repetition enhancement, although present at individual electrodes, did not survive group-level statistics in any region of interest.
span.quote: Group analyses aggregating recording sites with statistically significant repetition enhancement (RE) did not reach statistical significance for VOTC, LPFC, or OAS.

span.label: repetition suppression
span.quote: Repetition suppression, a decrease in cortical activation upon repeated stimulus exposure, has been widely observed under a variety of experimental conditions

span.label: behavioral priming
span.quote: Repeated stimulus exposure is also associated with faster and more accurate behavioral responses, referred to as “behavioral priming”.

span.label: event related causality (ERC)
span.quote: Event-related causality (ERC, implemented in custom analysis interface (ANIN) software ( Franaszczuk and Jouny, 2004 ), finds statistically significant event-related effective connectivity between ECoG recording sites using multivariate autoregressive (MVAR) models of ECoG activity in a subset of recorded signals.

span.label: predictive coding model (of repetition suppression)
span.quote: Given that perception relies on the integration of sensory information and prior expectations, the “predictive coding” model claims that repetition leads to optimized neural representations, with top-down activity serving as model-based predictions about the current stimulus and bottom-up activity representing the prediction error related to various stimuli and their constituent elements.

span.label: facilitation model
span.quote: The “facilitation” model ( James et al. , 2000 ; Henson, 2003 ) proposes that neural activity is advanced in time with repetition and terminates more rapidly.

span.label: synchrony model
span.quote: For example, the “synchrony” model ( Gotts, 2003 ; Ghuman et al. , 2008 ; Gilbert et al. , 2010 ) holds that neurons fire more synchronously after repetition while at overall reduced rates, improving the reliability of activity propagation.

span.label: stimulus repetition (novel vs. repeated picture)
span.quote: Two hundred fifty images were displayed in pseudo-randomized order, including 50 stimuli that were repeated identically after a short delay (100 trials total), either consecutively (no intervening stimulus) or with one different stimulus intervening between them.

span.label: naming response time
span.quote: Mean response times and their standard deviations, as well as median response times and median absolute deviations (MAD) for each patient for successful novel and repeated trials are shown in Table 2

span.label: high gamma power (70–120 Hz)
span.quote: An estimate of high gamma power at each time point in each trial was obtained by averaging the power in each bin between 70 and 120 Hz.

span.label: event-related causality (strength and direction of high gamma propagation between sites)
span.term: event-related causality (strength and direction of high gamma propagation between sites)
span.quote: Specifically, we tested for increases in responses to repeated stimuli as compared to novel stimuli, using a one-sided t-test with FDR correction.

span.label: word frequency of object names (matched) and repeated/novel list assignment (counterbalanced)
span.term: word frequency of object names (matched) and repeated/novel list assignment (counterbalanced)
span.quote: Object names were matched for word frequency, and lists of repeated versus non-repeated (novel) objects were counterbalanced across patients.

span.label: pre-stimulus baseline power (1 s before stimulus onset)
span.term: pre-stimulus baseline power (1 s before stimulus onset)
span.quote: In each signal, the power after stimulus onset was normalized to the baseline power from the 1 s prior to the stimulus onset, in each frequency bin.

span.label: t(9) = 6.015, p < 0.001 — Group-level paired t-test confirming faster responses to repeated than to novel pictures across the ten patients
span.quote: Behavioral priming effects were highly significant in a group analysis of all patients (paired t -test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons: t(9) = 6.015, p < 0.001, with each patient showing a numerical decrease in response time (RT) for repeated relative to novel trials (mean = 153 ms, and median = 128 ms).

span.label: 962 — Total number of recording sites sampled across all ten patients
span.quote: The anatomical distribution of these repetition effects was sampled with a total of 962 sites recorded across all 10 patients

span.label: 58 sites — Number of recording sites showing repetition suppression
span.quote: Repetition suppression (RS) was observed at 58 sites.

span.label: 30 sites — Number of recording sites showing repetition enhancement, none of them in VOTC
span.quote: Repetition enhancement (RE) was observed in 30 sites located in lateral frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, but not in VOTC.

span.label: 10 sites — Number of recording sites showing only a temporal shift in peak activation
span.quote: Temporal shift (TS) was observed in 10 sites, as noted above.

span.label: ~ 280 ms vs ~ 140 ms — Onset latency of significant repetition suppression in LPFC compared with VOTC
span.quote: Interestingly, in group analyses of repetition suppression (RS), it became statistically significant in LPFC later (~ 280 ms, Fig. 3 center) than in VOTC (~ 140 ms, Fig. 3 left), with a slight time-shift in the peak activation in LPFC to earlier time points in the repeat condition

span.label: 12–21 — Number of electrodes selected per patient for inclusion in the multivariate autoregressive model
span.quote: Using the aforementioned criteria, we selected 12–21 electrodes for inclusion in the MVAR model for each patient.

span.label: Ten patients — Sample size: epilepsy surgery patients with subdural ECoG who performed the object-naming task
span.quote: Ten patients provided informed consent to participate in experimental testing while electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded for epilepsy surgery under a Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board approved protocol.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pneurobio.2020.101788.
